theory_and_implementation: Python is the most widely used language for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning because of its readable syntax, extensive scientific libraries (NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow) and rapid prototyping capability. This lab revises the essentials of Python that will be used throughout the course: variables and data types, control flow, functions, and collections, followed by an introduction to NumPy, the fundamental package for numerical computing in Python.
Python is dynamically typed — a variable's type is inferred from the value assigned to it. Core built-in types include int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, dict and set.
Python uses indentation (not braces) to define blocks. The main control structures are conditional statements (if / elif / else) and loops (for, while).

Functions are defined using the def keyword and can accept default, positional, and keyword arguments. Functions are first-class objects in Python and can be passed around like any other value — an important property for later labs on agents and search, where functions represent actions, heuristics, and transition models.
"""Return True if n is a prime number."""
List comprehensions provide a concise way to build lists, and are heavily used in AI code for generating successor states, filtering candidate moves, etc.
squares = [x * x for x in range(10)]
evens = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]

NumPy (Numerical Python) provides the ndarray object, a fast, memory-efficient, multi-dimensional array, together with vectorized mathematical operations that avoid explicit Python-level loops. NumPy underlies almost every AI/ML library used later in this course (heuristic distance calculations, state vectors, reward matrices, transition matrices in MDPs, probability tables in Bayesian Networks, etc.).

Vectorized NumPy operations are typically an order of magnitude faster than an equivalent hand-written Python loop, because the loop is executed in optimized, compiled C code rather than the Python interpreter.

theory_and_implementation: What is an Agentic AI Tool?

Chapter 2 of this manual defined a rational agent as an entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it through actuators, choosing the action that maximizes its performance measure. An LLM agentic tool applies exactly this idea, but uses a Large Language Model as the reasoning core of the agent. Instead of hand-coded condition-action rules, the 'brain' of the agent is a language model capable of understanding natural-language goals, deciding which action (tool) to take next, observing the result, and repeating until the goal is achieved.
A typical agentic loop, popularised as the ReAct (Reason + Act) pattern, works as follows:
Thought: the LLM reasons in natural language about what it needs to do next.
Action: the LLM chooses a tool (a calculator, a web-search function, a database query, a Python REPL, etc.) and generates the arguments to call it with.
Observation: the tool executes and its output is fed back into the LLM's context.
The loop repeats until the LLM decides it has enough information to produce a Final Answer.
LangChain is a popular open-source framework that wraps raw LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, HuggingFace, local models via Ollama, etc.) with reusable abstractions needed to build agentic applications:
LLM / ChatModel wrapper — a uniform interface to call any underlying model provider.
PromptTemplate — parameterised prompt text that can be reused with different inputs.
Tool — a Python function (with a name and description) that the agent is allowed to call, e.g. a calculator, a search function, or a custom API call.
Agent / AgentExecutor — the component that runs the reasoning loop described above, deciding which tool to call and when to stop.
Memory — optional component that keeps track of the running conversation/history across steps.
This PEAS-style mapping helps connect the concept back to classical agents covered in Lab 3:
The user's natural-language prompt + tool outputs (observations)
Calling a tool (function) with generated arguments, or emitting a final answer
The tool-calling interface / API calls made by the agent
The LLM plus the prompt template that instructs it how to reason and act
Task success, accuracy of final answer, number of steps taken

Install LangChain and an LLM provider package. Any available provider may be used — a hosted API such as OpenAI, a free-tier hosted model, or a locally-run open model (e.g. via Ollama or HuggingFace transformers). The example below uses OpenAI-style syntax; substitute the provider available in the lab.
Step 1 — A minimal LLM call using a prompt template:
"You are an assistant for an AI course. Explain {topic} in two sentences."
prompt = template.format(topic="the difference between BFS and DFS")
Step 2 — Defining a Tool and building a tool-using agent:
"""Returns the number of letters in a word."""
description="Useful for evaluating arithmetic expressions like '23*7+1'"),
description="Useful for finding the number of letters in a word"),
agent.run("What is the length of the word 'Intelligence' multiplied by 12?")

With verbose=True, LangChain prints the full Thought / Action / Action Input / Observation trace, allowing students to see exactly how the agent decomposes the task, decides which tool to call, and combines intermediate observations into a final answer — this is the agentic loop in action.

theory_and_implementation: An agent is anything that can be viewed as perceiving its environment through sensors and acting upon that environment through actuators. A rational agent selects, at every instant, the action expected to maximize its performance measure, given the percept sequence observed so far and whatever built-in knowledge it has.
PEAS stands for Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors — the four elements needed to fully specify a task environment for an agent.
Amount of dirt cleaned, time taken, energy used
Correctness of reply, user satisfaction, response time
Two-square floor (A, B), each clean or dirty
Move Left, Move Right, Suck, NoOp

A simple reflex agent selects actions based only on the current percept, ignoring the rest of the percept history, using a set of condition-action rules of the form 'if condition then action'. It is the simplest of the five agent types (simple reflex, model-based reflex, goal-based, utility-based, learning agent) discussed in the lecture, and works well only in fully observable environments where the correct decision can be made based on the current percept alone.
static: rules, a set of condition-action rules

The vacuum-cleaner world has two locations, A and B, each of which may be Clean or Dirty. The agent perceives its current location and the dirt status of that location, and may choose to move Left, move Right, or Suck. The simple reflex rule is: if the current square is dirty, suck; otherwise, move to the other square.

theory_and_implementation: Depth-First Search can fail to terminate in infinite search spaces (or graphs with cycles) because it keeps expanding along a single branch. Depth-Limited Search solves this by supplying a depth limit, L: nodes at depth L are treated as if they had no successors, so the search never goes deeper than L. DLS is complete only if a solution exists at a depth ≤ L, and if L is chosen too small the search may report failure ('cutoff') even though a solution exists deeper in the tree.

Iterative-Deepening Search runs DLS repeatedly, increasing the depth limit L = 0, 1, 2, ... until a solution is found. It combines DFS's low memory footprint (O(bd)) with BFS's completeness and optimality (for unit step costs) — nodes at shallower levels are re-generated on every iteration, but this repeated work is asymptotically negligible because the number of nodes grows exponentially with depth (most of the work happens in the deepest, final iteration).

if result != cutoff then return result

When the search space is actually a graph (states can be reached via more than one path, or the state graph contains cycles), plain tree-search algorithms can loop forever by repeatedly re-visiting the same state. Repeated-state checking maintains an explored/visited set (or checks the current path for cycles) and refuses to re-expand a state already on the current path — this converts an (unbounded) tree search into a graph search.

if neighbor in path:            # repeated-state check on current path

theory_and_implementation: A heuristic function h(n) estimates the cost of the cheapest path from node n to a goal state. Heuristics inject problem-specific knowledge into the search, allowing informed search algorithms to explore far fewer nodes than uninformed search. A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true cost to the goal: h(n) ≤ h*(n) for every node n, where h*(n) is the actual optimal cost from n to the goal. A heuristic is consistent (monotonic) if, for every node n and successor n′ generated by action a with step cost c(n, a, n′), h(n) ≤ c(n, a, n′) + h(n′). Every consistent heuristic is admissible, but not vice-versa.

Two common heuristics used for grid/puzzle problems are: Manhattan distance — the sum of the horizontal and vertical distances between the current and goal position of every tile (admissible for the 8-puzzle, since each move only moves one tile one step); and Euclidean distance — the straight-line distance, commonly used for road-map path-finding.

Greedy Best-First Search expands the node that appears closest to the goal, using only the heuristic: f(n) = h(n). It is fast and uses relatively little memory, but is neither complete nor optimal in general, because it ignores the cost already incurred to reach n.

A* Search combines the path cost already incurred, g(n), with the heuristic estimate of the remaining cost, h(n): f(n) = g(n) + h(n). At every step, A* expands the node in the frontier with the lowest f(n). A* is complete, and is optimal provided the heuristic used is admissible (tree search) or consistent (graph search) — it will never expand a node whose f-value exceeds the optimal solution cost.

theory_and_implementation: The Minimax algorithm computes the optimal move for a player in a deterministic, fully-observable, two-player, turn-taking, zero-sum game, assuming the opponent also plays optimally. One player is MAX (tries to maximize the utility) and the other is MIN (tries to minimize it). Minimax performs a complete depth-first exploration of the game tree, evaluates terminal states with a utility function, and backs up (propagates) values from the leaves to the root: MAX nodes take the maximum of their children's values and MIN nodes take the minimum.

theory_and_implementation: Alpha-Beta pruning is an optimization of Minimax that prunes branches of the game tree that cannot possibly influence the final decision, without changing the result Minimax would have returned. It maintains two values while traversing the tree: α, the best value MAX can guarantee so far on the path to the root, and β, the best value MIN can guarantee so far. A branch is pruned (cut off) whenever α ≥ β, since neither player would ever allow the game to reach that branch.

if v <= alpha then return v     # prune

Part B — Expectiminimax for a Dice Game

Many games include an element of chance (a die roll, a card draw). Expectiminimax generalizes Minimax by adding CHANCE nodes between MAX and MIN nodes. At a CHANCE node, the backed-up value is the expected value over all possible outcomes, weighted by their probability: EXPECTIMINIMAX(n) = Σ P(outcome) × EXPECTIMINIMAX(RESULT(n, outcome)).
if node is a MAX node then return max over actions a of EXPECTIMINIMAX(RESULT(state,a))
if node is a MIN node then return min over actions a of EXPECTIMINIMAX(RESULT(state,a))
if node is a CHANCE node then
return sum over outcomes r of P(r) * EXPECTIMINIMAX(RESULT(state,r))

As a concrete example, consider a simplified two-player Pig-style dice game: on your turn you may ROLL a fair six-sided die (a CHANCE node: rolling a 1 ends your turn and scores 0 for this turn; rolling 2-6 adds that value to your turn total) or HOLD (a MAX/MIN decision node banking your current turn total and passing the turn). The agent must decide, for a given turn total, whether to ROLL again or HOLD, taking into account the probability distribution over die outcomes.

Part C — Introduction to Temporal-Difference (TD) Learning

Minimax and Expectiminimax both assume a perfectly known model of the game (transitions, utilities). Temporal-Difference learning instead lets an agent learn the value V(s) of states directly from experience, without needing a model of the environment. After each transition from state s to state s′ receiving reward r, the TD(0) update rule nudges V(s) toward the observed one-step return: V(s) ← V(s) + α [r + γ V(s′) − V(s)], where α is the learning rate and γ is the discount factor. The quantity δ = r + γ V(s′) − V(s) is called the TD error.

A solution is a complete, consistent assignment — one that assigns a value to every variable without violating any constraint. Unlike general state-space search, CSPs expose the internal structure of a state (a set of variable/value pairs), which allows general-purpose heuristics (rather than problem-specific ones) to be used.

Backtracking search is a depth-first search over partial assignments: it selects an unassigned variable, tries a value from its domain consistent with the constraints so far, and recurses; if no value works, it backtracks to the previous variable and tries another value. Backtracking search is systematic and complete for finite-domain CSPs.

theory_and_implementation: Forward checking is a simple form of constraint propagation performed during backtracking: whenever a variable X is assigned a value, forward checking removes any value from the domain of every unassigned variable connected to X by a constraint that would violate that constraint. If any domain becomes empty, the search backtracks immediately, avoiding wasted exploration further down the tree.

An arc X → Y is arc-consistent if, for every value x in the domain of X, there exists some value y in the domain of Y that satisfies the constraint between X and Y. The AC-3 algorithm maintains a queue of arcs and repeatedly makes each arc consistent (removing unsupported values from the tail variable's domain); whenever a domain is reduced, all arcs pointing into that variable are re-added to the queue, since they may no longer be consistent. theory_and_implementation: The conditional probability of event A given event B is defined as P(A | B) = P(A ∧ B) / P(B). Bayes' theorem, derived from this definition, allows a conditional probability to be 'inverted': P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B). In AI, Bayes' theorem lets an agent update a prior belief P(A) into a posterior belief P(A | B) after observing evidence B.

A Bayesian Network (BN) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in which each node represents a random variable and each directed edge represents a direct probabilistic dependency (a parent directly influences a child). Every node Xi is annotated with a Conditional Probability Table (CPT), P(Xi | Parents(Xi)), that quantifies the effect of the parents on that node. A BN compactly represents the full joint distribution over all the variables as the product: P(X1, ..., Xn) = Π P(Xi | Parents(Xi)). This factorization exploits conditional independence to represent joint distributions with far fewer parameters than a full joint probability table.
The classic textbook example is the 'Burglary Alarm' network: a Burglary or an Earthquake can trigger an Alarm, and the Alarm going off may cause John or Mary to call.
A burglary occurs at the house
John calls to report the alarm
Mary calls to report the alarm

pgmpy is a Python library for working with probabilistic graphical models, including Bayesian Networks; it supports defining the DAG structure, attaching CPTs, and performing exact/approximate inference (used in Lab 12).

theory_and_implementation: Inference in a Bayesian Network means computing the posterior distribution P(Query | Evidence) for some set of query variables given the observed values of some evidence variables, by summing (marginalizing) over all other ('hidden') variables. Inference is, in general, NP-hard, so both exact and approximate methods are used in practice.

Variable Elimination (VE) computes an exact answer to a query by writing the joint distribution as the product of CPTs (factors), and then eliminating (summing out) hidden variables one at a time, multiplying together all factors that mention the variable being eliminated and summing it out of the resulting product, before moving to the next hidden variable. This avoids the exponential blow-up of enumerating the entire joint distribution when the network structure allows factors to stay small.

Sampling-based methods estimate P(Query | Evidence) by generating many samples from the network's CPTs and using the empirical frequency of the query outcome among consistent samples as the estimate. Rejection sampling generates full samples from the network's prior distribution (using the CPTs in topological order) and simply discards (rejects) any sample that is inconsistent with the observed evidence, then estimates the query probability from the surviving samples. It is unbiased but can be very inefficient when the evidence is unlikely.

theory_and_implementation: A Hidden Markov Model models a system that transitions through a sequence of hidden (unobservable) states X1, X2, ..., Xt over time, obeying the Markov assumption (the current state depends only on the previous state), while each hidden state produces an observable emission Et that depends only on the current state. An HMM is fully specified by: the set of hidden states S; the set of possible observations O; the transition model P(Xt | Xt-1), usually given as a transition matrix A; the emission (sensor) model P(Et | Xt), given as an emission matrix B; and the initial state distribution π = P(X1).
The classic teaching example is inferring the weather (hidden: Rainy / Sunny) from whether a friend is observed to be carrying an Umbrella or not (observed) on each day.

The Forward algorithm computes the filtered belief P(Xt | e1:t) — the probability distribution over the current hidden state given all observations up to and including time t — recursively: α_t(j) = P(Et | Xt=j) · Σ_i α_{t-1}(i) · P(Xt=j | Xt-1=i), with α_1(j) = π(j) · P(E1 | X1=j). This runs in O(S² T) time, far better than summing over all S^T possible state sequences directly.

While the Forward algorithm sums over all paths to compute a marginal, the Viterbi algorithm finds the single most likely sequence of hidden states given the observations, argmax over X1:T of P(X1:T | e1:T), using the same dynamic-programming structure but replacing the sum with a max at each step, and keeping backpointers to reconstruct the optimal path once the end of the sequence is reached: δ_t(j) = P(Et | Xt=j) · max_i [δ_{t-1}(i) · P(Xt=j | Xt-1=i)].

theory_and_implementation: A Markov Decision Process is defined by a tuple (S, A, P, R, γ): a set of states S; a set of actions A; a transition model P(s' | s, a) giving the probability of reaching state s' after taking action a in state s; a reward function R(s, a, s') (or R(s)); and a discount factor γ ∈ [0, 1] that controls how much future rewards are worth relative to immediate rewards. Unlike the deterministic search problems of earlier labs, the outcome of an action in an MDP is stochastic — the same action taken in the same state may lead to different next states according to the transition probabilities.
Policies, Utilities and the Bellman Equation

A policy π(s) specifies the action to take in each state. The utility (value) of a state under policy π, Vπ(s), is the expected sum of discounted rewards obtained by following π from s onward. The optimal policy π* maximizes this value for every state. The optimal value function V*(s) satisfies the Bellman optimality equation:
V*(s) = max over a in A of [ Σ_{s'} P(s' | s, a) · ( R(s, a, s') + γ V*(s') ) ]

Value Iteration computes V* by iteratively applying the Bellman update to every state, starting from an arbitrary initial value function (typically all zeros), until the values converge (the maximum change between successive iterations drops below a small threshold ε). Once V* is known, the optimal policy is extracted by taking, in every state, the action that achieves the maximum in the Bellman equation.
function VALUE-ITERATION(mdp, epsilon) returns a utility function
V, V' = vectors of utilities for states in S, initially zero
for each state s in S do
V'[s] = max over a in A(s) of  sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) * (R(s,a,s') + gamma * V[s'])
if |V'[s] - V[s]| > delta then delta = |V'[s] - V[s]|

Policy Iteration alternates between two steps: policy evaluation, which computes Vπ for the current (fixed) policy π by solving the linear system Vπ(s) = Σ_{s'} P(s'|s,π(s))·(R(s,π(s),s') + γVπ(s')) (or approximately, via repeated Bellman updates without the max), and policy improvement, which updates π(s) to the action that is greedy with respect to the just-computed Vπ. The process repeats until the policy no longer changes, at which point it is guaranteed to be optimal.

Consider a robot car that wants to travel far and quickly without overheating. The car has two speeds, Slow and Fast, and two non-terminal states, Cool and Warm, plus a terminal Overheated ('dead-end') state. The transition model is: from Cool, driving Slow keeps the car Cool with probability 1.0; from Cool, driving Fast leads to Cool or Warm with equal probability 0.5 each. From Warm, driving Slow leads to Warm or Cool with equal probability 0.5 each; from Warm, driving Fast leads to Overheated with probability 1.0. Once Overheated, the car stays Overheated (absorbing state) with reward 0 thereafter. 15.title: Final Project Demonstration and Presentations
15.full_heading: Lab # 15: Final Project Demonstration and Presentations
15.software_required: As required by the chosen project
15.objective: To demonstrate, as a group, an end-to-end Artificial Intelligence system that integrates one or more of the techniques covered in this course (search, adversarial games, CSPs, probabilistic reasoning, or sequential decision-making) applied to a self-chosen, real or realistic problem, and to present the design, implementation and results to the instructor and peers.
tasks: 1.Clearly state the problem being solved and why it is a suitable application of one or more AI techniques covered in this course (e.g. an informed-search based route planner, a game-playing agent using Minimax/Alpha-Beta, a CSP-based scheduler/puzzle solver, a Bayesian-Network based diagnostic tool, or an MDP-based decision-making agent).

2.Formally model the problem in AI terms (state space and search formulation, or CSP variables/domains/constraints, or the network structure and CPTs, or the MDP's states/actions/rewards, as appropriate to the chosen technique).

3.Implement a working Python system, with a functional and reasonably user-friendly interface (command-line, notebook widgets, or a simple GUI/web interface) that lets the demonstrator run the system live.

4.Evaluate the system: report its performance (e.g. correctness/optimality of solutions, run-time or nodes explored, accuracy of inference, or achieved reward), and discuss any limitations or trade-offs made.

5.Reflect briefly on the ethical considerations relevant to the chosen application (fairness, transparency, safety, or misuse potential), in line with the Personal AI Ethics course-level outcome of this course.

   Approx. Duration

   Brief explanation of the AI model/technique used and key implementation decisions.
   Q&A
   3-5 minutes
   Instructor and peers ask questions to assess each member's understanding and individual contribution.

   Complete, runnable source code (submitted electronically as required by the instructor).
   A short project report covering: Purpose, AI technique(s) used and formal problem model, Implementation summary, Results/evaluation, and a brief ethical-considerations paragraph.
   Slides or notes used for the technical walkthrough.
   A statement of each group member's individual contribution.
   Evaluation
   This lab is evaluated using the Lab Rubrics (Group 6.1: Artificial Intelligence — Design and Analysis), the ED Open-Ended Lab Rubrics, and the Affective Lab Rubrics given at the beginning of this manual, covering problem understanding, demonstration and Q&A performance, adherence to instructions, completeness and accuracy of the working system, and — specific to the OEL rubric — model selection/training, deployment/UI quality, documentation, and reflective/ethical analysis.
   Summary
   This final lab consolidates the techniques learned across the semester — from Python and NumPy fundamentals, through agent design, classical and informed search, adversarial games, constraint satisfaction, and probabilistic and sequential decision-making — into a single, self-directed group project, giving students the opportunity to demonstrate independent design, implementation and critical evaluation of a complete AI system.
